routes.title: Paul's first journey
routes.yearNote: About AD 47-48, per the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's (1915) own stated span for Acts 13-14, within a wider ten-scholar range it reports running from before 45 (McGiffert) to 50-51 (Zahn). The famine-relief visit that precedes this journey (Acts 11:27-30) gives some background: the same encyclopedia's account of Paul's life places that visit at “the end of 44 or beginning of 45,” and its separate article on the famine itself dates the famine that “severely affected Palestine” to AD 45, without calling either date a fixed anchor for the journey that follows.
routes.note: Lines show stage order and land or sea mode, not exact traveled paths. Pisidia, Pamphylia and Lycaonia are regions the text names alongside the towns within them, not stops of their own. Paul's later letter to the Galatians is addressed to “the assemblies of Galatia,” and which congregations he meant has long been debated: the “South Galatian” view holds he wrote to the congregations this journey reaches, in the province's southern cities (Antioch in Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe); the “North Galatian” view holds he wrote instead to ethnically Galatian congregations further north, which this journey does not reach. This route takes neither side.

routes.title: Paul's second journey
routes.yearNote: About AD 46-53, per the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's (1915) stated span of “49-51 (or 52)” for Acts 15:36-18:22, within a wider ten-scholar range it reports running from 46 (McGiffert) to 50-53 (Ramsay). A Greek inscription from the emperor Claudius to the people of Delphi, dated to about AD 52, names Lucius Junius Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, the office Acts 18:12 records him holding; Acts 18:11 says Paul had by then spent eighteen months in Corinth, which the encyclopedia reads as “apparently” already true when Gallio arrived. The Society of Biblical Literature's Bible Odyssey project reads the inscription as placing Paul's stay in Corinth at 50-51; working from the same inscription, the encyclopedia instead places Gallio's arrival “either … the summer of 51 or 52 AD,” while cautioning that “we do not get a certain date as to the year.”
routes.note: Lines show stage order and land or sea mode, not exact traveled paths. Acts 16:6-8 names only regions (Phrygia and Galatia, then Mysia) between Lystra and Troas, and records that the party tried to enter Bithynia but was not allowed to; Bithynia is not recorded as a region passed through, since the text says they did not go there. As on the first journey, which congregations Paul's letter to the Galatians addresses is debated between those in the southern cities and others further north; this route does not take a side. Acts 18:22 says only that Paul “went up and greeted the assembly” between landing at Caesarea and going down to Antioch, without naming a city; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads this as probably Jerusalem, so this route records that stage as Caesarea to Antioch directly, with unknown travel mode.

routes.title: Paul's third journey
routes.yearNote: About AD 49-59: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's (1915) own account gives “52 (or 53)-57 (or 58) AD” for its own section covering Acts 18:23-21:14, three verses short of where this route ends (21:17; the boundary is discussed in the research note). Its wider ten-scholar range runs from 49 (McGiffert) to 53-59 (Clemen) for the journey itself, and from 53 to 59 for the arrest in Jerusalem that follows it, which together set this route's wider span.
routes.note: Lines show stage order and land or sea mode, not exact traveled paths. Acts 18:23 names “the region of Galatia and Phrygia,” reversing 16:6's order (“Phrygia and Galatia”); this route does not read significance into the reversal. As on the first journey, which congregations Paul's letter to the Galatians addresses is debated between those in the southern cities and others further north; this route does not take a side. Acts 20:1-6 names only regions between Ephesus and Philippi: Macedonia, then Achaia (which Acts also calls “Greece”), then Macedonia again on the return; no town is named for the three-month stay in Achaia, though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places a plot against Paul's life specifically in Corinth around this time. Acts 20:13 records that Paul himself went to Assos by land while his companions sailed there; this route records that stage as land, tracing Paul's own path, and the sailing instruction is in the quoted text. The stop at Trogyllium (Acts 20:15) is textually disputed: several early manuscripts omit the clause naming it, and some modern versions footnote it instead of printing it, but WEB includes it. One tradition has Paul landing near Lindos instead of the city of Rhodes (Acts 21:1); this route follows the city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's own account of this journey ends three verses earlier, at Acts 21:14; this route continues to the arrival itself, Acts 21:17, where Acts' own narrative turns to Paul's arrest.

routes.title: Paul's voyage to Rome
routes.yearNote: About AD 55-62: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reasons from the succession of the governor Festus (Acts 24:27) to place the sailing for Rome “in the late summer of 59 AD” and the arrival “in the early spring … of 60 AD.” Its wider ten-scholar range puts the arrival in Rome from 56 (McGiffert) to 62 (Clemen), with the voyage itself beginning the autumn before each scholar's arrival year (Acts 27:9, 28:11), which together set this route's wider span.
routes.note: Lines show stage order and land or sea mode, not exact traveled paths. Acts 27:1 does not itself name the port of departure; the preceding narrative places Paul in Roman custody at Caesarea (Acts 25:4, 25:13-27; 26:32), so this route treats Caesarea as the starting point on that basis. The ship's intended winter harbor, Phoenix, and the town of Lasea named near Fair Havens are not recorded as stops: the storm kept the ship from ever reaching Phoenix (27:12-15), and Lasea is named only as a landmark near Fair Havens (27:8). The sandbars called Syrtis (27:17) were feared, not reached, and are not a stop either. Acts 28:1 does not say which island “Melita” is; the traditional identification is Malta, which this route's line follows, while a minority view holds it was Mljet, off the Croatian coast. WEB reads “Clauda” at Acts 27:16; of six compared English versions, four (NIV, ESV, NLT, CSB) read “Cauda” instead, the form reflected in the island's modern Greek name, Gavdos, so this route titles the stop Cauda. WEB reads “The Market of Appius” at Acts 28:15; of six compared English versions, three (NIV, ESV, CSB) read “Forum of Appius,” two (KJV, NKJV) read “Appii Forum,” and one (NLT) reads only “the Forum,” so this route titles the stop Forum of Appius. Paul's party reached the Forum of Appius (43 Roman miles from Rome) before Three Taverns (33 Roman miles from Rome) while approaching the city, matching the order Acts 28:15 names them in.

scripture.textWEB: When it was determined that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan band.
The next day, we touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him permission to go to his friends and refresh himself.
Putting to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary.
When we had sailed across the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia.
When we had sailed slowly many days, and had come with difficulty opposite Cnidus, the wind not allowing us further, we sailed under the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone.
With difficulty sailing along it we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.

When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous because the Fast had now already gone by, Paul admonished them and said to them, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.” But the centurion gave more heed to the master and to the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul. Because the haven was not suitable to winter in, the majority advised going to sea from there, if by any means they could reach Phoenix and winter there, which is a port of Crete, looking southwest and northwest. When the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore. But before long, a stormy wind beat down from shore, which is called Euroclydon. When the ship was caught and couldn’t face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we were able, with difficulty, to secure the boat. After they had hoisted it up, they used cables to help reinforce the ship. Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, they lowered the sea anchor, and so were driven along. As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard. On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands. When neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope that we would be saved was now taken away. When they had been long without food, Paul stood up in the middle of them and said, “Sirs, you should have listened to me, and not have set sail from Crete and have gotten this injury and loss. Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I am and whom I serve, saying, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me. But we must run aground on a certain island.”

But when the fourteenth night had come, as we were driven back and forth in the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors surmised that they were drawing near to some land. They took soundings and found twenty fathoms. After a little while, they took soundings again, and found fifteen fathoms. Fearing that we would run aground on rocky ground, they let go four anchors from the stern, and wished for daylight. As the sailors were trying to flee out of the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they would lay out anchors from the bow, Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, “Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.” Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it fall off. While the day was coming on, Paul begged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you wait and continue fasting, having taken nothing. Therefore I beg you to take some food, for this is for your safety; for not a hair will perish from any of your heads.” When he had said this and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all; then he broke it and began to eat. Then they all cheered up, and they also took food. In all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship. When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. When it was day, they didn’t recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, and they decided to try to drive the ship onto it. Casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea, at the same time untying the rudder ropes. Hoisting up the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach. But coming to a place where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground. The bow struck and remained immovable, but the stern began to break up by the violence of the waves. The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim out and escape. But the centurion, desiring to save Paul, stopped them from their purpose, and commanded that those who could swim should throw themselves overboard first to go toward the land; and the rest should follow, some on planks and some on other things from the ship. So they all escaped safely to the land.
When we had escaped, then they learned that the island was called Malta.
After three months, we set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered in the island, whose figurehead was “The Twin Brothers.”
Touching at Syracuse, we stayed there three days.
From there we circled around and arrived at Rhegium. After one day, a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,
From there we circled around and arrived at Rhegium. After one day, a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,
where we found brothers, and were entreated to stay with them for seven days. So we came to Rome.
where we found brothers, and were entreated to stay with them for seven days. So we came to Rome.
From there the brothers, when they heard of us, came to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.
When we entered into Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard, but Paul was allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him.
